name: German Democratic Republic (East Germany)

areaKm2.note: Official GDR area 108,333 km2 incl. East Berlin (mid). The world_1960 East Germany polygon measures ~113,400 km2 on a spherical approximation (high).

population.note: COW NMC v7 tpop 1989 = 16,630 thousand (mid-year, incl. East Berlin). Low = end-1989 ~16.43M after ~340,000 people left during 1989.

urbanization.note: OWID/HYDE urban share Germany 1989 = 73.1% (whole Germany). GDR official statistics (towns of 2,000+) gave ~77% (high).

activePersonnel.note: Crane, RAND, East Germany's Military (1989) p. 34, citing IISS Military Balance 1987: 176,000 excluding border troops (army 120,000, navy 16,000, air force 40,000) plus 49,000 Border Troops. NVA article: 175,300 at the 1987 peak. Mid 173,000 allows the 10,000-man cut announced in January 1989. High 225,000 includes the Border Troops; COW NMC v7 milper 1989 = 262,000 also counts security troops.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: about 2.5 million men served 1956-1990 (NVA article); mobilisation planned four mobilisation divisions and two reserve divisions plus fillers (Land Forces article; Crane p. 34 notes four motor rifle divisions formed from reserves). IISS gave ~300,000 reserves (not fetched). Workers' militia Kampfgruppen (~200,000) excluded as paramilitary.

supportPersonnel.note: Active 173,000 minus infantry P roles (~34,000): navy 16,000, air force/air defence 40,000-44,000 (Crane p. 38; LSK article infobox 44,000), and the army's tank, artillery, air defence, engineer, signals and rear services.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess: same reasoning as the FRG: a 1989 general war would be short; the GDR could field ~0.5M in uniform plus militia (3%) at once, total war more.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess: dismounted motor rifle infantry of four motor rifle divisions and the motor rifle regiments of two tank divisions (Land Forces article: 1st, 4th, 8th, 11th MRD, 7th and 9th Panzer divisions); ~120,000 army personnel (Crane p. 34).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: BMP-1 and BTR-60/70 carriers, AK-74, RPG-7; BMP-2 only 24 (Land Forces article).

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: 18-month conscripts; NATO officers rated the NVA the best-trained Warsaw Pact army (NVA article).

count.note: Educated guess: Luftsturmregiment 40 (upgraded from a battalion in 1986, Land Forces article) and reconnaissance/special units.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: light airborne equipment.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: volunteers with longer service.

count.note: NVA article (BICC 1995): 2,199 artillery pieces handed over in 1990. Includes 2S1, 2S3 (95), D-30, D-20 (137), M-46 (175), BM-21 (72) and RM-70 (265) MRLs (Land Forces article).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: mix of SP 2S1/2S3 and towed guns; RM-70 MRLs.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Soviet artillery doctrine; Crane p. 36 notes GSFG had three times more artillery per unit.

count.note: NVA article (BICC Brief 3, Nassauer 1995): 2,761 tanks handed over in 1990 (mid). Low: Crane Table 11 (MB 1988) 1,700 T-54/55 and 350 T-72 with active units. Cumulative deliveries 2,099 T-55, 690 T-54, 583 T-72 (Land Forces article). High allows tanks in storage.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.25. Evidence: ~80% T-54/55 (some T-55AM2), only ~550 T-72M.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: conscript crews, high readiness, Soviet-style drills.

count.note: Land Forces article cumulative deliveries: BMP-1 1,133, BMP-2 24, BTR-60 2,260, BTR-70 1,316, MT-LB 721 = 5,454; older BTR-152/50/40 mostly retired by 1989. BRDM scout cars excluded. Mid allows attrition and retirements.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: BMP-1 and wheeled BTRs.

count.note: Crane Table 12 (Military Balance): 330 combat aircraft in 1987, of which >225 MiG-21 and 70 MiG-23. JG-3 converted to 24 MiG-29 in 1988-89 (LSK article; 24 MiG-29 passed to the Luftwaffe in 1990, NVA article). The LSK infobox figure of 800 combat aircraft counts trainers and helicopters.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: mostly MiG-21; few MiG-23ML and 24 MiG-29.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: tight ground-controlled interception, low flying hours.

count.note: Fighter-bomber wings JBG-37 (MiG-23BN) and JBG-77 (Su-22M-4) and naval MFG-28 (Su-22M-4), two squadrons each (LSK article), ~12-15 aircraft per squadron; Crane Table 12 shows 35 Su-22 added by 1987.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Su-22M-4 and MiG-23BN era-typical fighter-bombers.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript ground crews, limited low-level training.

count.note: Educated guess: NVA had 767 aircraft and helicopters in 1990 (NVA article); helicopters ~50 Mi-24, ~90 Mi-8, Mi-2 and ~13 Mi-14 naval.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Mi-24 attack helicopters.

count.note: Three Koni-class frigates (Rostock, Berlin, Halle), the largest Volksmarine ships (Volksmarine article; Crane p. 38).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.25-0.5. Evidence: export-model Koni with SA-N-4 and guns, no anti-ship missiles.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: conscript sailors, Baltic only.

count.note: Crane p. 38: ~160 ships, of which ~30 patrol craft and ~70 auxiliaries. Combatants: 15-16 Parchim corvettes, 5 Tarantul missile corvettes (Volksmarine article), ~12 Osa missile boats, ~30 Libelle/Shershen torpedo boats, ~25 Kondor minesweepers.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Tarantul with SS-N-2C, Parchim ASW corvettes new; torpedo boats dated.

count.note: Launchers: R-17 Scud (24 launchers plus decoys, retired 1990), 9K52 Luna-M (24 in service 1980), a few OTR-21 Tochka (Land Forces article). Nuclear warheads were Soviet-held.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Scud-B and FROG-7 inaccurate unguided or inertial missiles.

count.note: Batteries: LSK article lists ~31 Fla-Raketenabteilungen (S-75, S-125, S-200 fire units) in regiments FRR-13, -23, -31 and brigades; plus army divisional air defence regiments with 2K12 Kub, 9K33 Osa (41), Strela-1/10 and 131 ZSU-23-4 (Land Forces article) at ~5 batteries per division and an army 2K11 Krug brigade.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: dense Soviet-type SAM belt, mostly 1960s systems; S-200 long-range.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: integrated in the Warsaw Pact air defence system.

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5-0.75. Evidence: Soviet-trained staffs rated highly by NATO; but no national front command, NVA divisions under GSFG and Soviet army command in war (Crane p. 35); no war experience.

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.5. Evidence: SED-vetted officer corps, ~50% career soldiers (NVA article); conscript reliability doubtful once the regime crisis began in 1989.

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.25-0.5. Evidence: mass emigration from mid-1989; no units deployed against protesters in autumn 1989 (NVA article); fighting fellow Germans unpopular.

weapons.note: Anchor: between 8 (1943) and 9 (1985). Evidence: ATGMs, SAMs, T-72M and MiG-29 present, but most kit 1960s Soviet (T-55, MiG-21).

armor.note: Anchor: between 8 (RHA) and 9 (composite). Evidence: ~20% T-72M; T-55 RHA tanks dominant.

ships.note: Anchor: between 8 and 9. Evidence: missile corvettes and frigates without long-range missiles; no submarines.

fortification.note: Anchor: between 8 and 9. Evidence: hardened aircraft shelters, fortified border system (built against own citizens).

logistics.note: Anchor: between 8 (motor transport, rail) and 9. Evidence: 133,900 wheeled vehicles handed over 1990 (NVA article); rail-heavy Warsaw Pact logistics.

communications.note: Anchor: between 8 and 9. Evidence: Soviet-standard radio and troposcatter nets, Warsaw Pact automated air defence command.

isr.note: Anchor: between 8 (radar) and 9 (satellites). Evidence: radar networks, recon aircraft; Soviet satellite data only via GSFG.

air.note: Anchor: air 8 = 1943, 9 = 1985. Evidence: mostly MiG-21/MiG-23 (1960s-70s), 24 MiG-29.

cyber.note: Anchor: cyber 9 = 1990 networks. Evidence: Robotron computing years behind the West; Stasi signals intelligence but no military network operations.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison 2023 (OWID CSV, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true) Germany 1989 = 26,393 (2011 int$), split East/West with a per-capita ratio of 0.5 (range 0.4-0.6): CIA 1990 GDR GNP per capita $9,679 (Economy of East Germany article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_East_Germany) against FRG ~$19,000-20,000. With COW populations 62.06M/16.63M: East = r x 26,393 x 78.69 / (62.06 + r x 16.63) = 12,090-17,298.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Crane p. 33: reported defence budget 4.3% of GNP in 1980 (Collier estimate), 6.0% with state security; real spending grew faster than GNP into 1987-88 then flattened.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: CIA 1990 (Economy of East Germany infobox): 90% of GNP outside agriculture; industry was ~60-70% of net material product, ~50-55% of a Western-style GNP.

foodSurplus.note: Formula: foodSurplus = 1 - agricultural share of the labour force (share of food output not eaten by the farm population; no calorie self-sufficiency adjustment). CIA World Factbook 1990 (Project Gutenberg #14) labour force, GDR: 10.8% agriculture and forestry (1987). Share 10.8% (range 9.0-13.0%) -> 0.892 (0.87-0.91).

annualCohort.note: Educated guess: males reaching 18 in 1989 = 1971 birth cohort (~235,000 GDR births) x 0.513, minus mortality. Crane ch. IV: the GDR would need to conscript nearly all 18-year-old males in the early 1990s. Males only (conscript pool).

artillery.note: Educated guess: light weapons and some artillery ammunition and components only.

ifv_apc.note: Educated guess: no indigenous AFV lines; licence or repair capacity only. Tanks, aircraft and most weapons were imported from the USSR, CSSR and Poland (Crane ch. II: CSSR and Poland built T-72s under licence).

ships_minor.note: Educated guess: Peene-Werft Wolgast built Parchim corvettes and minesweepers at a few a year (Crane p. 38).

roadKm.note: Educated guess: ~47,000 km classified roads incl. ~1,850 km Autobahn; high includes municipal roads.

railKm.note: Educated guess: Deutsche Reichsbahn route network ~14,000 km in 1989, dense and heavily used for military transport.

majorPorts.note: Rostock (overseas port opened 1960, Economy of East Germany article), Wismar, Stralsund, Sassnitz/Mukran (rail ferry to the USSR from 1986).

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Deutsche Seereederei Rostock fleet ~1.3-1.5M GRT, x1.5 dwt/GRT.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess: Warsaw Pact front logistics, rail-fed, NVA divisions attached to Soviet armies.

nuclearWarheads.note: FAS stockpile series (OWID) lists no East German warheads. Soviet nuclear warheads stored in the GDR for NVA delivery systems (Scud, FROG, Su-22) under Soviet custody belong to the ussr-1989 snapshot.

chokepoints: Berlin and its encircled western sectors

homeDefense.note: 1.1 row: familiar terrain and local supply, rail network, border fortifications; population support uncertain in 1989; no strategic depth.

notes: Snapshot date mid-1989 (IISS Military Balance 1989-90 reference date 1 July 1989), before the November 1989 collapse. Main source: Keith Crane, East Germany's Military: Forces and Expenditures, RAND Arroyo Center report (Oct 1989, isbn 0-8330-1033-6), fetched as DTIC ADA221839 full text on archive.org; it quotes IISS Military Balance 1987-88 figures. Equipment totals cross-checked with the 1990 handover inventory (NVA article, BICC Brief 3): 767 aircraft, 208 ships, 2,761 tanks, 2,199 artillery pieces. The January 1989 Warsaw Pact force data statement was not fetched. Border Troops (~47,000-49,000) and Kampfgruppen militia excluded from active (border troops in the high range). The 19-20 Soviet divisions of the GSFG (~380,000 troops) stationed in the GDR are counted in ussr-1989. Population includes East Berlin.
